newsitem.title: CHILE: CHILE DECLARES CATASTROPHE TO FIGHT FLOODS, SNOW.
newsitem.headline: CHILE DECLARES CATASTROPHE TO FIGHT FLOODS, SNOW.

text.p: Chile declared a "state of catastrophe" on Monday in Santiago and seven central regions because of heavy rains and flooding that have forced about 51,000 people to flee their homes.

Interior Minister Carlos Figueroa announced the measure covering a vast area from the Atacama desert to about 497 miles (800 km) south of the capital Santiago. The declaration will release special government funds for flood relief.
"The catastrophe area is enormous and has forced us to put all the state's resources toward helping those people affected," said Figueroa after a crisis meeting with President Eduardo Frei.

Demands for help to repair houses and provide aid including blankets, mattresses, food and medicine already total close to $3 million and are rising by the hour, said Figueroa, who heads government efforts to deal with the emergency.
New blizzards at the Argentine border forced Chilean rescuers on Monday to suspend efforts to rescue about 200 people trapped by heavy snow since Thursday.

With roads blocked by 18 feet (six metres) of snow, the 200 travelers were holed up in a customs office and nearby buildings at Los Libertadores pass with adequate food and heating but no word on when they could leave.
"There is a tremendous snowstorm in the mountains. No helicopter in the world could fly through it," an air force officer said.

Wind gusts reached 44 mph (70 kph) and visibility was near zero, a National Emergency Office spokesman said. He said it was doubtful rescue efforts could be resumed on Monday at the pass, the main land route between Argentina and Chile.

The travelers, mainly Chileans, Argentines and Peruvians, were heading through the narrow pass in trucks, cars and buses when the blizzard hit on Thursday, forcing most of them to stop at the customs building. Others were trapped in the Cristo Redentor tunnel under the border or at a ski resort a few miles down the road.

Torrential rains and strong winds have been buffeting central Chile since Thursday, dumping massive snowfalls at high elevations, flooding towns and forcing thousands to leave their homes, many of them in Santiago's low-lying western outskirts.

"We're facing a weather front that is extraordinarily tough ... and we will need special efforts to overcome its effects," said Frei after visiting flood victims in the Santiago suburb of San Bernardo.

The town of Maipu, one of the worst-hit areas, was under up to 3 feet (one meter) of water after nearby rivers burst their banks, but most people refused to leave their houses for fear of looting, residents said.
At least 17 deaths have been blamed on floods since early June. Public Works Minister Ricardo Lagos said the floods had done about $70 million in damage to highways and bridges.
But Figueroa called on politicians and the media to stop "alarmist" reporting on the floods, accusing some local officials of deliberately exaggerating the effects of floods to get more relief money.

Local news reports have linked the bad weather to El Nino, a cyclical warm current in the Pacific Ocean that has been linked this year to unusually hot weather in Peru and strange weather patterns elsewhere.
